problemText: The Equator is an imaginary line that runs around Earth. What does the Equator separate?
choices: The North Pole from the South Pole
The Eastern Hemisphere from the Western Hemisphere
The Northern Hemisphere from the Southern Hemisphere
The Prime Meridian into two equal parts
hints: Think about which pair of hemispheres has 'north' and 'south' in their names.
The Equator runs east and west around the middle of Earth.

problemText: A student marks a point on a globe that sits directly south of the Equator and directly east of the Prime Meridian. Use the two-question method to determine which two hemispheres contain this point. First ask whether it is north or south of the Equator, then ask whether it is east or west of the Prime Meridian.
choices: Northern Hemisphere and Western Hemisphere
Southern Hemisphere and Western Hemisphere
Northern Hemisphere and Eastern Hemisphere
Southern Hemisphere and Eastern Hemisphere
hints: South of the Equator means Southern; east of the Prime Meridian means Eastern.
Always apply the north-south question first, then the east-west question.

problemText: A traveler flies east from Europe and crosses the Prime Meridian while heading in that direction. On which side of the Prime Meridian is the traveler now, and which hemisphere does that put them in?
choices: East of the Prime Meridian, in the Eastern Hemisphere
West of the Prime Meridian, in the Western Hemisphere
East of the Prime Meridian, in the Western Hemisphere
West of the Prime Meridian, in the Eastern Hemisphere
hints: When you cross a line while heading in a direction, you end up on that side of the line.
The Eastern Hemisphere is on the east side of the Prime Meridian.

problemText: A mountain range lies entirely between the Equator and the North Pole, and it is entirely west of the Prime Meridian. Which hemispheres have no land from this mountain range in them?
choices: Northern Hemisphere and Western Hemisphere
Southern Hemisphere and Eastern Hemisphere
Southern Hemisphere and Western Hemisphere
Eastern Hemisphere and Western Hemisphere
hints: If a place is north of the Equator, it cannot be in the Southern Hemisphere.
If a place is west of the Prime Meridian, it cannot be in the Eastern Hemisphere.

problemText: A continent has land both north and south of the Equator, but no land crosses the Prime Meridian. In how many of the four hemispheres does this continent have land?
choices: One hemisphere only
Three hemispheres only
Two hemispheres only
All four hemispheres
hints: Since the continent does not cross the Prime Meridian, it is on only one side of that line.
Since it crosses the Equator, it is on both sides of that line. Remember that a place sits in one hemisphere from each pair.

problemText: Two geographers argue about South America. One says it must be in exactly two hemispheres because all places on Earth are in exactly two hemispheres. The other says South America is in three hemispheres. Use what you know about how many lines cross South America and where those lines run to explain which geographer is correct and why the other one made an error.
choices: The second geographer is correct. South America straddles both the Equator and the Prime Meridian, and when both lines cross a continent, that continent must occupy all four hemispheres.

The second geographer is correct. The Prime Meridian crosses South America, dividing it into eastern and western parts, while the entire continent is south of the Equator, giving it land in three hemispheres total.

The first geographer is correct. Every place and every area on Earth is limited to exactly two hemispheres, one from the north-south pair and one from the east-west pair, and this rule has no exceptions.
The first geographer is correct. South America lies entirely south of the Equator and entirely west of the Prime Meridian, so only one line crosses it, leaving it in exactly two hemispheres.
hints: Recall that a single point sits in exactly two hemispheres, but a large area can spread across a line.
For South America specifically, check whether the Equator crosses it or stays on only one side of it, and check whether the Prime Meridian crosses it or stays on only one side of it.

problemText: You are looking at a map and you want to know what place or topic the entire map is about. Which of these four parts of the map should you look at to answer that question?
choices: The scale bar
The legend
The compass rose
The title
hints: This part is made of words printed on the map, usually near the top.
This part names the exact place or subject the map shows.

problemText: A student is holding a map titled 'Riverside Park Map.' She looks at the legend and sees that a small green square stands for a playground and a small blue diamond stands for a water fountain. Later, she finds a green square symbol on the map itself. What does that symbol represent on this particular map?
choices: A playground, because the legend pairs a green square with that meaning
A water fountain, because water features are always shown in green on every map ever made
A park entrance, because symbols in titles and on maps always match the same category
A picnic area, because green squares are standard symbols for outdoor recreation spaces
hints: Each map makes its own choice about what each symbol means.
Check only the legend to find out what a symbol stands for on this map.

problemText: You are measuring two points on a map using a ruler. The two points are 4 inches apart on the page. You want to know about how far apart those two places really are in the real world. Which part of the map gives you this information?
choices: The title, which names the location shown and helps identify which map you are using
The scale bar, which connects distances on the map to real-world distances
The compass rose, which shows the directions on the map and helps with orientation
The legend, which lists what each symbol means and helps you decode the symbols
hints: This part is a marked bar that shows what a length on the page equals in the real world.
The answer is the only part that connects page measurements to actual distances.

problemText: A student studying the Mountain Trail Map notices that the compass rose has an arrow labeled N pointing toward the right side of the page. On the map itself, a tent symbol sits directly to the left of a cabin symbol. Based on the compass rose shown on this map, in which direction does the cabin lie from the tent?
choices: East, because the cabin is to the right on the page and this map shows north pointing to the right
West, because the cabin is to the left on the page and left always indicates a westward direction
East, because the compass rose shows north pointing right, so left is west
South, because the cabin appears lower on the page than the tent symbol
hints: Always use the compass rose printed on the map itself, not a compass rose you remember from another map.
If north points right on this map, then left on this map points in the opposite direction.

problemText: A map of Hickory Forest shows a legend with a brown dashed line labeled 'hiking trail,' a compass rose with N pointing upward, and a scale bar marked 0 at the left end and 2 miles at the right end. A hiker looks at the map and finds two hiking trails marked with the dashed lines. One trail appears to run northward along the top half of the map, and another runs southward along the bottom. The hiker measures the top trail with a ruler and finds it spans the entire length of the scale bar. Which statement is correct?
choices: The top trail is about 2 miles long, and the bottom trail runs east because it is below the first trail
The top trail is about 2 miles long, and both trails must run in the same direction because they are the same symbol
The top trail is about 2 miles long, but the map does not tell you which direction the bottom trail runs
The top trail is about 2 miles long, and it runs north because the compass rose shows N pointing upward
hints: Use the scale bar to find the length and the compass rose to find the direction.
The compass rose tells you the direction a trail runs; the symbol alone does not.

problemText: A student receives four different maps to study: Map 1 is titled 'Downtown Shopping District,' Map 2 is titled 'State Park Hiking Routes,' Map 3 is titled 'Bus Stop Locations,' and Map 4 is titled 'County Forest Trails.' The student has a question: 'What does the red circle symbol stand for on the map I am looking at right now?' The student does not know which map she is holding. Which of the following is the most accurate statement about how to answer this question?
choices: Check the legend on the map in front of you, because each map chooses its own symbols and their meanings
Check the compass rose, because the direction a symbol points reveals its meaning
Check the title first, because it names what the map shows and that tells you what symbols will appear
Check the scale bar, because symbols are only meaningful if the map has accurate distance measurements
hints: What a symbol means depends on the legend of the specific map you are holding, not on the title or content.
A red circle might mean something different on each of these four different maps.

problemText: A map's legend shows a star inside a circle to mark capital cities, thin black lines to show borders between countries, and different flat colors filling in each country. What is the main job this map is built to do?
choices: Show the human-made boundaries and place names of countries and cities.
Display how high or low the land sits across different elevations.
Show how much rainfall falls in each part of the country during a year.
Illustrate which natural features such as rivers and mountains are located where.
hints: Look at what the legend actually lists: borders, a capital-city marker, and country colors.
Ask yourself: does the legend describe the shape of the land, data spread across an area, or human-made places and boundaries?

problemText: A geographer wants to study which areas of a region have the most people living in them. She creates a map where light tan means 'fewer than 10 people per square mile,' medium brown means '10 to 50 people per square mile,' and dark brown means 'more than 50 people per square mile.' What type of map has she made, and why does that map type fit her purpose?
choices: A political map, because different colors help separate one country from another country and the legend lists borders, capitals, and place names.
A thematic map, because it shows how one chosen kind of information — population spread — changes from place to place.
A physical map, because brown colors on a map always show elevation and the shape of the land using height and terrain symbols.
A climate map, because the map uses different shades of color to represent data values that vary across different geographic regions.
hints: The legend does not list borders or capitals, and it does not list elevation colors. Eliminate those two map types first.
What single topic does the legend track across the whole region? Is that the definition of a thematic map?

problemText: Two students are looking at the same country on a map. One student says, 'I can see green in the south and brown in the north, so the south must be flatter and the north must be mountains.' The legend, however, lists green for 'wheat-growing areas' and brown for 'dairy-farming areas.' Is the student's reasoning correct, and what type of map is this really?
choices: Yes, the student is correct, because green on a physical map always means low elevation and brown always means highland terrain.
No, the student made an error by assuming green always shows flatland and brown always shows mountains when used on physical maps showing elevation zones.
No, the student assumed the colors show elevation, but the legend lists what type of farming is done in each area instead. This is a thematic map.
No, because the student did not check the legend first to see what the brown and green colors were actually meant to represent on this particular map.
hints: Do not guess the map type from the colors alone. Read what the legend actually says the colors stand for.
Physical-map colors stand for elevation. What do these colors really stand for according to the legend?

problemText: A student looks at three different maps of the same country. The first legend lists elevation colors — green for low and brown for high — plus mountain-peak symbols. The second legend lists country borders, capital cities, and state borders. The third legend lists a single color scale showing temperature ranges from cool to hot across all regions. The student claims, 'The country looks completely different on each map because mapmakers are bad at their jobs.' Explain why the student's reasoning is wrong and why the maps actually look different.
choices: The maps look different because mapmakers use different colors and symbols arbitrarily without following any real rules or standards.
The maps look different because one is a physical map and two are political maps, so the physical map stands out visually.
The maps look different because the country's actual geography and borders changed between the time each map was made.

The maps look different because each map is built around a different legend to show a different kind of information — one shows natural landforms, one shows political boundaries, and one shows data about temperature. Each map type has a different job.
hints: Remember that every map is built around one main job. What is the job of each of the three legends described?
A political map, physical map, and thematic map of the same place would not look alike. Why not?

problemText: A teacher gives four students a blank map of a region and asks each student to create a map. Student A creates a legend listing which type of mineral is mined in each area. Student B creates a legend listing rivers, mountain peaks, and elevation colors. Student C creates a legend listing administrative region borders and capital cities. Student D creates a legend listing which language is most commonly spoken in each area. Which two students created thematic maps?
choices: Students A and B, because thematic maps use color and symbols more effectively to display information than other map types.
Students A and D, because each legend shows one chosen kind of information spread across different areas.
Students B and C, because physical maps and political maps are the most common types created in geography classes.
Students C and D, because these maps focus on human features such as cities, languages, and cultures rather than landforms.
hints: Identify what each legend is built to show. Does each one list a single chosen topic spread across the area, or does it list something else?

Student A's map shows mining areas — one type of data spread across a region. Student D's map shows languages — also one type of data spread across a region. What do these two have in common that the others don't?

problemText: Three maps of the same forest region exist. Map 1's legend shows elevation colors and river symbols. Map 2's legend shows 'protected wildlife areas' in green and 'areas open to logging' in yellow. Map 3's legend shows county borders, town names, and a capital marked with a star. A ranger asks, 'Which map should I use to find out where the mountains are?' A land-use planner asks, 'Which map shows me where forests can be cut down?' A government official asks, 'Where is the county boundary line between these two counties?' For each question, which map answers it best, and why does the other two not fit?
choices: Map 1 answers all three questions because it shows the most information at once, making it the most practical choice for all users regardless of what they need to know.

Map 1 answers the ranger's question (it shows natural landforms); Map 2 answers the planner's question (it shows one chosen data topic spread across the area); Map 3 answers the official's question (it shows human-made boundaries). Each map has a legend built for a different purpose.
Map 2 answers all three questions because it shows both the natural features and the human-made divisions needed to locate mountains, logging zones, and county lines.

Map 1 answers the ranger's question because it displays elevation; Map 2 answers both the planner's question and the official's question since it shows land-use data including conservation boundaries that align with county lines.
hints: For each question, decide which map's legend is built to answer it. What single piece of information does each person need — landforms, land use, or human-made boundaries?

Remember: a physical map shows elevation and natural features; a thematic map shows one chosen topic; a political map shows boundaries and place names. Match the job to the map type, then match the question to the job.

problemText: A continent is defined as one of Earth's largest continuous areas of land. Using the seven-continent convention, how many continents are there on Earth?
choices: Six
Seven
Five
Four
hints: The seven-continent convention divides Earth into these landmasses: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America.
Count each continent in the list above.

problemText: A student is told that Australia is completely surrounded by ocean and has no land connection to any other continent. Which of the following best explains why Australia is still called a continent rather than just an island?
choices: Because explorers who first arrived there decided to name it a continent, and that decision was recorded in early maps and voyage journals.
Because Australia covers more total area than any single island on Earth, and geographers needed a different term for landmasses above a certain size threshold.
Because it is one of Earth's largest continuous areas of land, which is the definition of a continent.
Because it is located in the Southern Hemisphere opposite to the Arctic Ocean, placing it in a geographic zone reserved for continents.
hints: A continent is defined by size and being a continuous area of land, not by whether water surrounds it.
Size and continuous land area matter more than whether an ocean separates a landmass from others.

problemText: Europe and Asia sit on the same continuous landmass with no ocean or sea between them, yet geographers still count them as two separate continents instead of one. What does this situation demonstrate?
choices: That two continents can only be separated when a body of water like an ocean or sea creates a physical barrier between them.
That Europe and Asia were historically considered one continent for thousands of years before being split into two for political reasons.
That continents must always be divided by narrow strips of land in order for them to be counted as separate geographic regions.
That the division of continents is a convention—a way people agreed to divide Earth—rather than a natural division marked by water.
hints: A convention is an agreement people made that could have been done differently—not a rule of nature.
Some continents are separated by oceans or water, but Europe and Asia show that continents can be divided in other ways too.

problemText: To describe where a continent or ocean is located, geographers use a two-question method: First, identify what continents or landmasses touch the location's edges. Then, specify the direction (north, south, east, or west) in which each neighbor lies relative to that location. Apply this method to describe the location of the Arctic Ocean. What is the correct description?
choices: North America, Europe, and Asia all border the Arctic Ocean; they lie to the south of the Arctic Ocean.
The Arctic Ocean touches Australia to the east, Antarctica to the south, and Africa to the west.
The Atlantic and Pacific Oceans border the Arctic Ocean; the Atlantic lies to the east and the Pacific lies to the west.
The Arctic Ocean is surrounded on all sides by the southern edges of the four major oceans, with no continents nearby.
hints: The Arctic Ocean is located at the far northern end of Earth.
If continents border the Arctic Ocean to its north, then the Arctic Ocean is to their south—directions flip when reversed.

problemText: A student claims that because Africa and Asia are joined by a continuous landmass with no water between them, they must be neighboring continents in the same way that North America and South America are neighboring continents. Is this claim correct? Explain why or why not based on how these pairs are actually connected.
choices: Yes, the claim is correct. Both pairs of continents touch each other along their borders, so the type or width of the connection between them does not matter for determining if they are neighbors.

No, the claim is incorrect. Africa and Asia share a continuous landmass with no water between them, while North America and South America are connected by only a narrow strip of land, which is a different type of connection.

No, the claim is incorrect. The connection between Africa and Asia is narrower than the connection between North and South America, making them less closely related as neighboring continents despite both pairs being connected.

Yes, the claim is correct. Since both pairs of continents are physically attached to each other without water separating them, they share the same relationship as neighbors regardless of whether the landmass connecting them is wide or narrow.
hints: Europe and Asia are joined by a large continuous landmass, while the Americas are connected by a narrow strip of land—these are two different types of connections.
Two continents can touch in different ways: sharing a large continuous landmass or being connected by a narrow strip of land.

problemText: A student writes three location statements: (1) The Indian Ocean has Africa to its west and Asia to its north. (2) South America lies west of the Atlantic Ocean. (3) Antarctica is surrounded by the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans. For each statement, apply the two-question method and use the direction-flip test to determine which statements are correct and which contain an error in direction or in naming neighbors.
choices: Statements (1) and (2) are correct; statement (3) is incorrect because Antarctica is surrounded by all three oceans and also sits below the southern edges of the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian, not just surrounded by them.
Statement (1) is incorrect because Asia lies to the east of the Indian Ocean; statements (2) and (3) are correct.
Statements (1) and (3) are correct; statement (2) is incorrect because South America lies east of the Atlantic Ocean, not west.
All three statements are correct when checked against the positions of the continents and oceans.
hints: For each statement, flip it to test if the reverse direction also makes sense: if X is west of Y, then Y must be east of X.
Check statement (2) carefully: if the Atlantic Ocean lies between the Americas and Europe/Africa, which side of that ocean is South America on?
